# LangGraph 1.x Changes During 2025–2026

## Release Timeline and Stability

LangGraph 1.0 alpha launched in mid-2025 alongside LangChain 1.0 alpha for both Python and JavaScript, with the stable 1.0 release targeting late October 2025 [1][5]. Notably, the alpha proved stable enough that developers did not need to restructure existing code when migrating to stable [5]. The release came with a formal stability commitment guaranteeing no breaking changes until a future v2.0, establishing LangGraph as a production-ready framework [4].

## Core Philosophy and Architecture

The guiding principle of the 1.x line was "shrink surface area, harden the runtime" [1]. LangGraph became the underlying execution engine for LangChain 1.0's new `create_agent` abstraction, creating a clean separation: `create_agent` handles standard tool-calling loops while raw LangGraph provides explicit workflow control [4]. Several components were deprecated in favor of this unified model, including `create_react_agent`, `AgentState`, `AgentStatePydantic`, `ValidationNode`, and `MessageGraph` [6]. Python 3.9 support was also dropped, requiring Python 3.10 or higher [6].

## Production Runtime Enhancements

The 1.x line hardened several production-facing capabilities. Core features included deterministic concurrency, checkpointing for persistence, human-in-the-loop via `interrupt()`, and time-travel functionality enabling resume, branching, and auditing from any prior checkpoint [1].

## Later Incremental Improvements (v1.2.0)

Subsequent patch releases added meaningful capabilities. Version 1.2.0 introduced per-node timeouts via `run_timeout` and `idle_timeout` options, node-level error handlers for recovery and compensation patterns, and graceful shutdown that saves resumable checkpoints [2]. A new beta `DeltaChannel` type was added to store only incremental deltas rather than full state snapshots, reducing checkpoint overhead for long-running threads with large data such as message lists [2]. Additionally, a version 3 event streaming API was launched with a content-block-centric protocol and typed per-channel projections including `run.values`, `run.messages`, `run.lifecycle`, and `run.subgraphs` [2].

Taken together, the 1.x line transformed LangGraph from an experimental tool into a stable, operationally mature framework purpose-built for durable, controllable agent execution [4][1].
